text:
Poundland has called in administrators putting 12,000 jobs at risk ahead of Christmas after its owners rejected at least two last-ditch bids for the budget retailer.
Administrators at AlixPartners have been appointed to the retailer, which has 600 stores in the UK and Ireland by Poundland’s directors. The chain is now expected to be broken up with significant job losses and store closures.
Alix Partners said a sales process “did not identify a viable solvent solution for the business as a whole”.
The retailer’s US owner, Gordon Brothers, which bought Poundland for a nominal £1 last year, has been under pressure to accept an offer that would save jobs and protect thousands of the retailer’s suppliers.
High inflation and heavy competition from budget stores, online specialists and supermarkets have left the 36-year-old retailer – the UK’s first and biggest nationwide single-price retailer – struggling.
The retailer’s board filed a notice of intention to appoint administrations last month – which was later extended – protecting Poundland from the demands of creditors until 26 November while a solution to its problems was sought.
Just two bidders interested in the whole company remained in talks right up until this week’s deadline.
Martin Property Group, a Northern Irish family-owned company, which has been working with the existing management, led by Barry Williams, for about two months, remained interested.
It was joined by a last-ditch bid from Germany’s Zachert Private Equity, a fund founded by a former Bloomberg journalist that specialises in acquiring mid-sized companies such as the German photo studio group Studioline and the US food and drink company Brands Within Reach.
Other bidders for the whole group included the little-known finance group Xyra Group Holdings, and the Irish investment company Innovest, which both fell out of the bidding race over the past week.
The company’s board was forced to appoint administrators before Thursday’s deadline as shelves began to empty because it was running short of funds to restock during its peak Christmas trading period.
Gordon Brothers’ UK director, Mark Newton-Jones, held the latest of several meetings with the business secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, on Monday, more than a week after giving evidence to parliament’s business select committee after MPs called on the government to protect Poundland and other high street stores from “predatory capitalism” and asset-stripping last week.
Poundland, founded with one store in Burton upon Trent in 1990, was the first UK-wide chain based on a single price. Poundland has endured a rocky history under a string of different owners as it has faced rising costs and heavy competition from chains such as Savers, Home Bargains and B&M, as well as from the big supermarkets.
It is now expected to be broken up with retailers such as Poundstretcher, B&M and The Range taking parcels of stores.
Gordon Brothers rejected an initial management-backed rescue bid financed by Martin Property Group for the discount chain. It bought the struggling chain from the European retail group Pepco in June 2025.
The US-based finance company said that it could raise more from a breakup of Poundland, selling off stock and parcels of stores to rival retailers, than through the first bids promised only a small upfront payment for the £30m in shareholder debts that Gordon Brothers took on with its fellow shareholder – Poundland’s former owner, Pepco.
The deals were rejected by Gordon Brothers despite Pepco, which holds £7.5m of the debt, saying it was prepared to wait for repayment in the hope of saving the business.
